    Building Agentic Diagnostic Tools

    A practical, field-tested playbook for teams building similar agentic diagnostic workflows: architecture, technology choices, LLM mechanics, human validation, reliability watch-outs, and reuse guidance.

    Purpose

    This document front-loads the questions other teams are likely to ask when they try to understand how OPs-AI-Agents built agentic diagnostic workflows. It is not a full architecture specification. It is a field guide: what we chose, why we chose it, what worked, what hurt, and what to watch when adapting the pattern.

    Use this doc when:

    • A new team asks how to build a diagnostic tool with LLMs, files, and human validation.
    • A PR introduces a new agent workflow and needs to explain why it follows the existing pattern.
    • A team wants to copy parts of OPs-AI-Agents and needs to know which parts are reusable versus project-specific.
    • We need a shared language for questions around token usage, provider choice, streaming, file parsing, job state, and admin-managed knowledge.

    Executive TL;DR

    If you only read one page, take these five points:

    PrincipleWhat it means in this repo
    Workflow over chatThe product is built around case/process/plant workflows, not a free-form chatbot surface.
    Backend owns orchestrationFastAPI routes call services, services coordinate DB/file/agent work, and agents run as local Python packages.
    Frontend never talks to internalsBrowser calls go through Next.js API proxy routes; BACKEND_BASE_URL stays server-side.
    State must survive the model callFiles, extracted evidence, validation decisions, benchmark versions, and stage outputs live in PostgreSQL/S3 or local storage.
    Humans validate business truthThe agent can draft, parse, classify, score, and synthesize, but consultant/admin decisions are explicit persisted product events.

    Repo Architecture At A Glance

    Browser UI
  -> Next.js 16 App Router
  -> Next.js API proxy routes (/api/backend, /api/streaming, /api/workflows)
  -> FastAPI backend (/api/v1)
  -> Backend service layer + SQLAlchemy models + Pydantic schemas
  -> Editable local agent packages in services/agent/*
  -> PostgreSQL + S3/local file storage + Anthropic/OpenAI APIs

    The important repo-specific point: agent packages are not separate HTTP services. They are installed into the backend as editable local dependencies via uv.sources, then called in-process by backend services/routes.

    Watch-out This makes streaming and local development simpler, but long-running/high-concurrency workflows need durable job state and shared concurrency control across backend replicas.

    LLM Ops Checklist

    Before a workflow is production-ready, answer these questions:

    TopicQuestion
    TimeoutIs there an explicit timeout for every LLM/provider call?
    RetryIs there a bounded retry policy for transient failures?
    ConcurrencyIs maximum concurrency defined per workflow stage and deployment topology?
    Token budgetAre input/output token estimates logged or measurable?
    ProvenanceIs the model/provider/version stored for durable outputs?
    ValidationAre structured outputs validated before persistence?
    Failure modeIs there a degraded/partial-failure state for batch workflows?
    Provider policyIs there a clear path for direct APIs vs Bedrock/internal gateways?

    Build Sequence

    1. Define the business workflow contract and the human decision points.
    2. Define typed schemas for every stage output.
    3. Build file/data ingestion and source traceability first.
    4. Add the smallest useful agent stage.
    5. Persist job/stage status and user validation decisions.
    6. Add review UI before expanding automation.
    7. Add observability, retry/timeout policy, and regression tests.
    8. Only then scale concurrency or add additional agent stages.

    Executive Summary

    OPs-AI-Agents is built around structured advisory workflows, not open-ended chat. The platform takes consultant-managed case data, client files, and domain rubrics, then produces typed outputs that can be reviewed, adjusted, and eventually used in client-facing deliverables.

    The most important design choice is that agents are part of a product workflow. They are not isolated demos. Every agent output needs:

    • A typed schema.
    • A persisted source of truth.
    • A human review surface.
    • A way to trace back to source data.
    • A failure mode that is visible to the user.
    • A way to re-run or repair without losing validated work.

    Reference Architecture

    The repo is a monorepo with three runtime layers and several local agent packages:

    services/frontend/   Next.js 16 App Router UI + server-side API proxy routes
services/backend/    FastAPI API, SQLAlchemy/Pydantic domain layer, file storage, orchestration
services/agent/      Editable local Python packages imported by the backend at runtime

    System design diagram

    The real runtime flow in this repo: browser to Next.js proxy, FastAPI orchestration, local agent packages, durable storage, and external model providers.

    UI Layer
    Consultant / AdminRuns diagnostics, validates outputs, maintains knowledge workflows.
    Browser UINext.js pages, review surfaces, Data Manager, streaming components.
    Next.js 16 App Routerservices/frontend/src/app, product pages, client components, Zustand stores.
    API proxy routes/api/backend, /api/streaming, /api/workflows; no direct browser access to BACKEND_BASE_URL.
    Service And Agents Layer
    FastAPI /api/v1HTTP route handlers in services/backend/api/v1/routes.
    Backend service layerCases, Data Manager, maturity, baselining, benchmarks, access/admin workflows.
    Domain contractsSQLAlchemy models, Pydantic schemas, Alembic migrations.
    Editable local agentsagent_sdk, maturity_assessment, measure_generation, scrap_diagnostic, and related domain agents.
    Data Layer
    PostgreSQLCases, files metadata, evidence, stage outputs, validation decisions, versions.
    S3 / local uploadsOriginal uploaded files and generated artifacts via backend file storage abstraction.
    Admin knowledge dataVersioned benchmark/definition rows, dry-run reports, publish history.
    External
    Anthropic / OpenAIHosted LLM APIs used by agent workflows today.
    Enterprise gatewaysPotential future Bedrock/internal gateway route for provider access and policy.
    Infrastructure authSSO/gateway behavior is handled outside the app code path.

    Deployment Topology

    Deployment is intentionally separated from the runtime system diagram: the product path is browser -> proxy -> backend -> agents/data/providers, while deployment explains how those runtimes are packaged and shipped.

    Backend imageFastAPI plus editable agent packages are built into one runtime container, so agents ride with the backend process.
    Frontend imageNext.js standalone output is built and deployed as a separate frontend container.
    Helm / Octopus / KubernetesPrimary deployment path uses Docker images, BCG SMP base charts, Helm packaging, and Octopus releases.
    EC2 pathSecondary deployment path uses Docker Compose for selected environments.
    Secrets and storageRuntime secrets are injected via platform mechanisms; file storage points to S3 or local storage depending on environment.
    Scaling watch-outBackend replicas scale API and agent capacity together, so long-running agent jobs need durable state and shared concurrency controls.

    Runtime Request Paths

    FlowPath through the repoNotes
    Standard CRUDBrowser -> Next.js /api/backend/* -> FastAPI route -> service -> SQLAlchemy -> PostgreSQLUsed for cases, processes, plants, admin screens, and most persisted data.
    File upload / Data ManagerBrowser -> proxy -> backend Data Manager routes -> file storage service -> S3/local + DB metadataOriginal files live in storage; parsed/semantic state lives in DB.
    Maturity assessment pipelineBackend route/service -> services/agent/maturity_assessment LangGraph pipeline -> LLM calls -> persisted MA outputsStructured pipeline: parse/extract/score/gap/synthesis with human validation surfaces.
    Baselining / streaming extractionBrowser SSE consumer -> /api/streaming/* proxy -> backend streaming routes -> helix_agent_sdk agent loopSSE is the live transport; DB state is still needed for durable recovery.
    Measure generation / quantificationBackend services -> services/agent/measure_generation -> persisted measure candidates/quantificationsLLM proposal generation plus typed formulas/calculation contracts.
    Admin knowledge workflowsAdmin UI -> backend admin services -> validation/dry-run/publish -> versioned DB rowsUsed for benchmark and definition maintenance by Knowledge Admins.

    Boundary Rules

    Browser -> backendBrowser calls only Next.js proxy routes, never BACKEND_BASE_URL directly.
    Backend -> agentsBackend imports local agent packages; agents do not expose HTTP servers.
    Agents -> backendAgent packages should not import backend route/service code.
    Durable statePostgreSQL and S3/local storage are the source of truth.
    LLM providersProvider calls need timeout, retry, provenance, and token policy.
    DeploymentFrontend/backend are containerized; agent packages ride inside the backend image.

    Package Layout That Matters

    PathResponsibility
    services/frontend/src/appApp Router pages and API proxy routes.
    services/frontend/src/componentsProduct UI, review surfaces, Data Manager, streaming UI.
    services/frontend/src/lib/apiPreferred typed frontend API client and endpoint wrappers.
    services/backend/api/v1/routesHTTP route handlers; should stay thin.
    services/backend/servicesBusiness logic, orchestration, file handling, admin workflows.
    services/backend/modelsSQLAlchemy ORM models.
    services/backend/schemasPydantic API contracts.
    services/backend/alembic/versionsDatabase migration history; keep one linear head unless intentionally merged.
    services/agent/agent_sdkCurrent default extraction engine and streaming-oriented agent runtime.
    services/agent/maturity_assessmentLangGraph-based maturity parsing/extraction/scoring/synthesis.
    services/agent/measure_generationMeasure proposal, refinement, and quantification agent logic.
    services/agent/scrap_diagnosticScrap diagnostic package.
    services/agent/data_request / siop_value_potential / interview_agentAdditional domain agents/workflows.

    The deliberate choice is to run agent packages in-process inside the backend rather than as separate network services. This keeps streaming and human-in-the-loop flows simple and low-latency. The tradeoff is that backend pods also carry agent CPU, memory, token, and concurrency load.

    Core Technology Choices

    ChoiceWhy we chose itWatch-out
    FastAPI backendTyped Python API layer, strong ecosystem, easy async/sync integrationRoutes can become too large unless service boundaries are enforced
    Next.js frontendProduct UI, server-side API proxy, deployable standalone appKeep backend URLs server-side only
    PostgreSQLShared source of truth for cases, files, outputs, validationsUse explicit migrations and watch Alembic head collisions
    SQLAlchemyORM and query controlAvoid returning lazy ORM relationships outside session scope
    S3 / local file storage abstractionSame code path can run locally and in deployed environmentsMissing source files must be surfaced as user-visible failures
    LangGraphGood fit for staged pipelines like parse -> extract -> score -> synthesizeKeep graph state typed and small
    Agent SDK / in-process agentsLow-latency orchestration and direct SSE/event integrationBackend resource usage scales with agent workload
    SSESimple server-to-client streaming for agent progressDoes not replace durable job state
    Pydantic schemasRuntime validation and stable API contractsAvoid accepting free-form LLM JSON without schema validation
    Instructor / structured outputConverts LLM responses into typed modelsStill needs retries, timeouts, and schema evolution discipline

    LLM Fit Assessment

    Before designing an agent, evaluate whether the workflow needs an LLM at all. The best diagnostic products use LLMs for ambiguity, language, synthesis, and judgment support, while keeping deterministic parsing, validation, calculations, routing, and persistence outside the model.

    Start with the value testBe explicit about whether the LLM adds speed, reliability, coverage, or reduces tedious semantic review work.
    Use LLMs for ambiguityMessy source text, evidence extraction, synthesis, contradiction detection, and user-facing explanations.
    Prefer code for certaintyCalculations, schema validation, date/unit normalization, deduplication, routing, access checks, and status transitions.
    Design hybrid stagesLet deterministic code prepare bounded context, then let the LLM handle the semantic step, then validate again.
    Reassess after MVPIf behavior stabilizes, move it from prompts into scripts, services, rules, or database constraints.

    Decision Rule

    QuestionIf yesIf no
    Does the LLM make the workflow faster, more reliable, broader in coverage, or materially less tedious for humans?Continue evaluating an agentic workflow, especially when the task involves semantic review of large or unstructured inputs.Prefer manual, template-based, rules-based, or deterministic implementation.
    Does the task require interpreting ambiguous language, messy documents, or consultant-style reasoning?Consider an LLM stage with strong input bounds and evidence traceability.Use deterministic code, SQL, schemas, or rules.
    Can the expected output be fully specified as a calculation, lookup, state transition, or validation rule?Do not use an LLM for the core logic; reserve it only for explanation if needed.Use an LLM only for the part that cannot be expressed reliably as code.
    Would the same input need to produce the same output every time for audit or compliance?Prefer deterministic implementation, or add human approval before persistence.LLM variance may be acceptable if outputs are validated and reversible.
    Is the model being asked because the data is poorly structured?First improve parsing, metadata, templates, or admin-managed taxonomy where feasible.Proceed with the simplest reliable implementation path.
    Can a human quickly verify the output with source evidence?LLM assistance can be safe if review state is explicit.Avoid autonomous LLM writes; require stronger validation or a non-LLM path.

    Non-LLM First Patterns

    • Use Pydantic and database constraints for shape, type, and referential integrity.
    • Use deterministic scripts for spreadsheet normalization, unit conversion, and formula evaluation.
    • Use rules or taxonomy tables for stable classification decisions that admins can maintain.
    • Use search, retrieval, and ranking before asking a model to reason over a large context.
    • Use human-in-the-loop review when the model output can change business recommendations.
    A useful rule of thumb: if the workflow needs judgment, language understanding, or synthesis, an LLM may belong in the loop. If it needs correctness, repeatability, authorization, or accounting, keep that responsibility in code and let the model assist around it.

    Agent Workflow Patterns

    Use three workflow shapes in this repo: pipeline agents for known stage boundaries, human-in-the-loop agents when ambiguity must be resolved before continuing, and admin-managed knowledge workflows when non-engineers need safe ownership of changing domain content.

    Pattern 01

    Structured Pipeline Agents

    Best for workflows with known stages, such as maturity assessment parsing, contradiction detection, measure generation, and quantification.

    Use when: the workflow can be decomposed into deterministic stage boundaries with typed handoffs.

    Input files / case state
  -> parse / normalize
  -> extract structured evidence
  -> score or calculate
  -> synthesize
  -> persist typed outputs
  -> expose review UI

    Structured pipeline shape

    Input contextCase/process/plant state, files, rubrics, prior validated outputs.
    Parse / normalizeTurn source material into ordered, traceable working context.
    ExtractLLM-assisted structured evidence, candidates, or observations.
    Validate schemaPydantic / typed contracts reject malformed output before persistence.
    Score / synthesizeCalculate, rank, cluster, score, or summarize by stage contract.
    Persist + reviewWrite durable outputs and expose consultant validation UI.
    Pattern 02

    Interactive Human-in-the-Loop Agents

    Best for workflows where the agent needs clarification before it can safely continue, such as baselining discovery or file/table mapping.

    Use when: uncertainty affects correctness and the right next step is a specific consultant/admin decision.

    Start session
  -> agent inspects files
  -> agent asks a specific question
  -> backend persists waiting state
  -> frontend asks user
  -> user answers
  -> agent resumes
  -> result is validated and persisted

    Ask, persist, resume loop

    Agent runtime
    Inspect filesRead workbook/document context and detect ambiguity.
    Ask targeted questionSheet, metric, mapping, unit, period, or confidence clarification.
    Resume safelyContinue only after a persisted answer resolves the blocker.
    Product state
    Persist waiting stateSession is recoverable; stream alone is not the source of truth.
    User answerFrontend captures the decision and sends it back through backend APIs.
    Validated resultFinal output is stored and reviewable after the loop completes.
    Do not hide uncertainty. If the agent cannot determine a mapping safely, ask.
    Pattern 03

    Admin-Managed Knowledge Workflows

    Best when domain content changes over time and non-engineers need ownership, such as maturity benchmarks, industry definitions, or data item taxonomies.

    Use when: the product needs dry-run validation, publish controls, version history, and rollback semantics.

    Seed initial data via migration
  -> expose admin UI
  -> dry-run upload / edit
  -> validate
  -> publish new version
  -> keep history and rollback path

    Dry-run, publish, version

    Seed / importMigration seed, Excel upload, or admin edit creates a proposed change set.
    Dry-run validationUnknown dimensions, bad numeric values, hierarchy mismatches, and duplicates are surfaced before writes.
    Reject / repairAdmin fixes the source data without changing active production rows.
    PublishValidated rows become the new active version with a durable audit trail.
    v1inactive history
    v2inactive history
    v3active global / scoped row
    rollbackreactivate prior version when supported

    Excel seed files are acceptable for bootstrapping. They should not become the long-term editing interface if Knowledge Admins need to maintain the data.

    How We Leverage Claude Skills for the MVP Feature Set

    Skills are our MVP packaging layer for domain-heavy agent work. They let us keep workflow instructions, references, scripts, schemas, and validation close to the diagnostic capability, while the durable product boundary remains the backend service, typed schemas, persisted state, and review UI.

    Keep

    Claude Skills pattern

    Local skill packages with SKILL.md, references, scripts, schemas, and manifests. This is the reusable pattern for fast domain workflow development.

    Legacy

    Anthropic Skills API / Files API

    The older cloud-container execution path under services/agent/streaming. Useful historically, but not the default for new work.

    Current

    Agent SDK skill runtime

    The current extraction direction under services/agent/agent_sdk: skills load locally and execute through the in-process Agent SDK pipeline.

    MVP Use Cases

    01
    Add a baseline quicklyCreate a new skills/{skill_id} folder instead of rewriting the orchestrator.
    02
    Keep domain rules maintainableStore instructions in SKILL.md and references instead of scattering them across Python services.
    03
    Reuse the stage shapeMost baseline skills follow discovery -> preprocessing -> classification.
    04
    Add deterministic helpersShip Excel inspection, preprocessing, validators, and preview builders with the skill.
    05
    Bound output qualityPair skill instructions with Pydantic models and validation scripts.
    06
    Support HITL momentsInstruct the agent when to ask clarification questions or show previews before final persistence.

    Current Skill Runtime Shape

    Skill package to validated output

    Skill foldermanifest.yaml, SKILL.md, references, scripts, assets.
    Load contextskill_loader and manifest loading assemble stage instructions.
    Agent SDK orchestratorRuns in backend process and delegates stage work.
    Stage subagentsDiscovery, preprocessing, classification with stage-specific tools.
    MCP + validationQuestions, previews, DB persistence, scripts, Pydantic checks.
    Durable outputValidated rows/results stored in PostgreSQL and linked to files/session state.

    What Goes Into a Skill

    manifest.yamlDeclares the skill, stage list, stage folders, tools, models, and orchestration metadata.
    1-discover/SKILL.mdTeaches the discovery agent how to inspect the file and describe available signals.
    2-preprocess/SKILL.mdDefines preprocessing expectations; much of this should stay shared across skills.
    3-classify/SKILL.mdContains the most domain-specific classification rules.
    references/*.mdDomain definitions, taxonomy, classification guidance, output format notes.
    scripts/*.py + modelsDeterministic helpers, validators, and Pydantic models/enums for stage outputs.

    Watch-outs Before Scaling Beyond MVP

    Prompt sprawlDuplicated SKILL.md files drift across baseline types.Mitigation: extract shared discovery/preprocessing instructions and inject only skill-specific hints.
    Token pressureLarge reference files and examples can dilute stage focus.Mitigation: keep stage-scoped prompts and load only relevant references per stage.
    Weak runtime sandboxingAgent SDK skills run locally in the backend container, not in Anthropic's isolated Skills API container.Mitigation: use command safety hooks, working-directory restrictions, Docker isolation, and avoid user-provided code execution.
    Validation gapsA good prompt is not a contract.Mitigation: validate every stage output with Pydantic/scripts before persistence.
    Version driftSkill changes can alter behavior without obvious product migration.Mitigation: track skill/model/prompt versions in outputs and add regression fixtures.
    Too much logic in promptsPrompt-only workflows become brittle.Mitigation: promote stable transformations into Python scripts or backend services.

    Recommendation for Other Teams

    Use Claude Skills as the MVP packaging pattern when the workflow is domain-heavy, file-heavy, and still evolving. Do not treat Skills as a replacement for product architecture. Durable boundaries still need backend services, typed schemas, persisted state, validation UI, and observable job status.

    LLM Usage Mechanics

    Read this section as the operating model for model calls: pick the provider path deliberately, keep prompts bounded, validate every output, and store enough provenance to explain business results later.

    Provider pathSeparate model capability from enterprise access route: direct APIs, Bedrock, Azure, or internal gateways.
    Token budgetConstrain context by stage and load only the rubric/files needed for the current decision.
    ConcurrencyParallel calls need shared limits across replicas, not just in-memory counters.
    ProvenancePersist model, prompt family, rubric/benchmark version, files, and user overrides.

    Provider Access

    The codebase currently uses direct provider APIs in several places, primarily Anthropic and some OpenAI usage. This was pragmatic for speed and SDK support.

    For future teams, separate these decisions:

    • Model capability: which model produces the best output.
    • Provider interface: direct API, Bedrock, Azure, internal gateway, or another enterprise-approved route.
    • Operational policy: timeouts, retries, logging, secrets, rate limits, and cost tracking.

    If switching to AWS Bedrock or another provider gateway, expect more effort than changing one client constructor. The work usually includes:

    • A provider abstraction layer.
    • Model ID / parameter mapping.
    • Streaming differences.
    • Tool/function-call differences.
    • Error and retry mapping.
    • Token accounting changes.
    • Regression tests for structured outputs.
    • Prompt compatibility checks.

    Token Budgeting

    Token usage grows faster than expected because diagnostic workflows combine:

    • System prompts.
    • Domain instructions.
    • Rubric text.
    • Uploaded file excerpts.
    • Conversation history.
    • User corrections.
    • Structured output examples.
    • Previous stage outputs.

    Practical rules:

    • Treat prompt size as an engineering budget, not a model detail.
    • Log or estimate input and output tokens per call.
    • Keep long rubrics outside every prompt unless needed.
    • Pass only the dimensions, files, rows, or evidence relevant to the current stage.
    • Prefer chunked extraction over one enormous prompt.
    • Use summaries cautiously; summaries can remove auditability.
    • Store enough metadata to explain why a result was produced.

    Concurrency and Rate Limits

    Parallel LLM calls improve throughput but can overload:

    • LLM provider rate limits.
    • Backend CPU and memory.
    • Database connection pools.
    • S3/file IO.
    • Browser polling or SSE connections.

    Recommended controls:

    • Per-stage concurrency limits.
    • Per-tenant or per-case concurrency limits when needed.
    • Backpressure when the system is already busy.
    • Explicit timeouts for all external calls.
    • Retry with bounded exponential backoff for transient provider failures.
    • A clear degraded state when some batches fail.

    In multi-replica deployments, in-memory concurrency limits are not enough. Each pod enforces its own limit, so the total system concurrency can exceed the intended cap. Use shared coordination for production-grade limits, such as PostgreSQL row locks, Redis counters, or a queue/worker model.

    Structured Output

    Use typed output wherever possible.

    Good pattern:

    LLM response
  -> Pydantic model
  -> validation
  -> database write
  -> API response schema
  -> frontend rendering

    Avoid:

    • Free-form JSON parsing.
    • Persisting malformed LLM output and hoping downstream code handles it.
    • Letting None silently mean both "not present" and "invalid".
    • Treating schema validation as a frontend-only concern.

    Prompt Versioning

    Prompt changes can change business outputs. For important workflows, store enough information to reconstruct:

    • Which prompt family produced the output.
    • Which model was used.
    • Which rubric/benchmark/version was used.
    • Which source files and evidence were included.
    • Which user overrides were applied.

    This does not mean every prompt edit needs a database migration. It does mean durable outputs should not be impossible to explain later.

    Human-in-the-Loop Validation

    Human validation is a first-class product boundary: the system should make it clear what the agent inferred, what the human accepted or changed, and which downstream outputs are now safe to trust.

    1. Source relevanceConfirm files, sheets, pages, and diagnostic scope before extraction.
    2. Entity mappingResolve plant, process, period, currency, unit, and metric ambiguity.
    3. PreviewShow extracted rows/evidence before expensive scoring or synthesis.
    4. AssumptionsValidate calculations, normalization, exclusions, and overrides.
    5. ApprovalPersist final user decision and mark downstream state as trustworthy.

    Agentic diagnostics need human validation as a product primitive, not as a nice-to-have.

    Recommended principles:

    • Separate raw agent output from user-validated output.
    • Persist user decisions explicitly.
    • Make "not relevant", "validated", "excluded", and "reset" states unambiguous.
    • Show source evidence next to generated conclusions.
    • Let users correct inputs before re-running expensive downstream stages.
    • Make destructive reset/regenerate actions less prominent and clearly named.
    • Preserve enough history to explain how the current state was reached.

    Common failure modes:

    • A re-run deletes user-entered work.
    • A reset partially resets some derived rows but leaves hidden exclusions.
    • A user thinks they validated a whole stage but only validated one card.
    • The UI says a job completed while part of the pipeline degraded.
    • The agent asks broad questions when it should ask a concrete, answerable one.

    For baselining-style flows, human validation should happen at stage boundaries:

    1. File selection and data relevance.
    2. Entity mapping, such as plant, process, period, currency, units.
    3. Metric extraction preview.
    4. Calculation / normalization assumptions.
    5. Final baseline approval.

    Each boundary should have a persisted status and a clear "what happens next" action.

    Data and File Mechanics

    Files are not just uploads; they are source-of-truth objects that need ownership, assignments, parsing lineage, evidence traceability, and safe repair semantics.

    RegisterCase ownership, process/step assignment, labels, storage key.
    ParseRead document or workbook with stable ordering metadata.
    ExtractCreate evidence, observations, rows, or candidate outputs.
    TraceLink outputs back to document, page/slide, segment, paragraph, and block.
    RepairStage replacement parse before deleting validated downstream work.

    Data Manager as the File Source of Truth

    Uploaded files should be registered once and then reused by diagnostic steps. A file should have:

    • Case ownership.
    • Optional process assignment.
    • Diagnostic-step assignment.
    • Storage location.
    • Classification labels.
    • Validation status.
    • Lineage where applicable.

    Agents should not rely on ad hoc local paths as durable references. Local paths are execution details. The durable reference is the registered file row plus its storage key.

    Parsing and Evidence Traceability

    Document pipelines should preserve reading order and traceability.

    Recommended metadata:

    • Document ID.
    • Segment index.
    • Paragraph index.
    • Block index.
    • Page/slide where available.
    • Source filename.
    • Character offsets where available.
    • Stable UUID as tie-breaker only, never as primary reading order.

    Important lesson: UUIDs are identifiers, not ordering. If code previously sorted integer IDs to preserve context, a UUID migration can silently randomize ordering. Add strict validation immediately after parsing so missing or malformed ordering metadata is caught early.

    Re-parse and Repair

    Re-parse flows are dangerous because they often delete existing parse trees, evidence, scores, and derived outputs.

    Safe pattern:

    Resolve source files
  -> pre-validate availability and parseability
  -> stage replacement parse
  -> swap old rows only after replacement succeeds
  -> invalidate downstream outputs explicitly
  -> show user what was reset

    Avoid deleting good existing evidence before proving the replacement parse can succeed.

    Excel and Master Data

    Excel is useful for bootstrapping and bulk admin upload, but it needs guardrails:

    • Dry-run before publish.
    • Explicit validation errors for non-numeric cells, missing sheets, duplicated rows, and unknown IDs.
    • No silent coercion of invalid values to null.
    • Versioned publish.
    • Ability to see active version and history.
    • Role-gated admin UI for non-engineer maintenance.

    The migration should seed initial data. Ongoing business ownership should live in an admin workflow.

    Reliability and Operational Watch-outs

    The reliability question is less “did the model answer?” and more “can the product recover, explain, retry, cancel, and avoid corrupting validated state?”

    Job statePersist status and stage transitions; in-memory state is not enough for production.
    Partial failureRepresent degraded, waiting, cancelled, stale, and failed states explicitly.
    External callsEvery provider/storage/notification call needs timeout, retry policy, and user-visible errors.
    MigrationsAlembic head collisions are a team workflow issue; catch them in CI before merge.

    Job State

    In-memory job state is easy to build and easy to lose.

    It is acceptable for prototypes and short local tasks. It is risky for production workflows where users expect resumability.

    Watch-outs:

    • Pod restart loses job status.
    • Multi-replica deployments can route polling to a different pod.
    • Background tasks can continue after the original request context is gone.
    • A job can partially write outputs and then fail before updating status.

    Preferred direction:

    • Persist job records in PostgreSQL.
    • Store stage, status, timestamps, warnings, and error details.
    • Make jobs idempotent or safely retryable.
    • Use durable worker/queue patterns for long-running tasks when feasible.

    Partial Failure

    Diagnostic pipelines should distinguish:

    • Success.
    • Failed.
    • Completed with warnings / degraded.
    • Waiting for user input.
    • Cancelled.
    • Stale because upstream data changed.

    Do not collapse all non-happy paths into 500s or completed jobs.

    External Calls

    Every external call should have:

    • Explicit timeout.
    • Retry policy where safe.
    • Error classification.
    • User-visible failure message.
    • Structured logging.

    External calls include:

    • LLM providers.
    • S3.
    • OCR/PDF parsing libraries when they access external services.
    • Notification systems.
    • Transcription APIs.

    Database Migrations

    This repo has repeatedly seen Alembic branch collisions. Other teams should expect this if multiple feature branches add migrations in parallel.

    Mitigations:

    • CI check for unexpected multiple heads.
    • Rebase migrations onto current dev before merge.
    • Use clear migration ownership in large PRs.
    • Prefer unique revision IDs over human-numbered filenames when practical.
    • Keep downgrade semantics honest. If downgrade is unsupported, say so explicitly.

    Background Work

    Avoid mixing many background execution patterns unless there is a clear reason. This repo currently has examples of:

    • FastAPI background tasks.
    • In-memory job dictionaries.
    • Async tasks for streaming workflows.
    • Threaded or graph-based agent execution.

    The long-term shape should converge toward fewer patterns with shared status tracking and shared cancellation semantics.

    Security and Compliance Watch-outs

    Treat prompts, intermediate files, parsed evidence, and generated outputs as sensitive client data unless proven otherwise. The safest default is to minimize logging and keep provider access server-side.

    Prompt/data loggingDo not log full client documents or full prompts by default.
    Server-side secretsKeep provider keys and backend URLs out of browser-visible code.
    Role-gated adminAdmin knowledge workflows need explicit role controls and auditability.

    Agentic diagnostic tools often process sensitive client data. Treat prompts and intermediate outputs as potentially sensitive.

    Watch-outs:

    • Do not log full client documents or full prompts by default.
    • Avoid leaking backend/internal URLs to the browser.
    • Keep provider API keys server-side only.
    • Gate admin knowledge-management endpoints by role.
    • Separate client-uploaded raw files from processed outputs.
    • Define retention and deletion behavior for files, parse trees, and generated evidence.
    • Consider whether LLM provider terms and region/data-boundary requirements match the case context.

    When moving from direct provider APIs to enterprise-hosted routes such as Bedrock, validate not only connectivity but also logging, data retention, model availability, and structured-output behavior.

    Testing and Evaluation

    Agentic systems need the normal test pyramid plus workflow evaluation: deterministic seams for parsing/calculation/persistence, fixture coverage for files, and LLM evals for prompt quality.

    Deterministic testsParsers, validators, schemas, calculations, and status transitions.
    Fixture testsRepresentative DOCX/PPTX/PDF/XLSX files with edge cases.
    Golden outputsExpected outputs for deterministic pipeline stages.
    LLM evalsPrompt quality and regression tracking outside live-model happy paths.

    Agentic tools need both normal software tests and workflow-specific evaluation.

    Recommended layers:

    LayerPurpose
    Unit testsPure parsing, calculation, validators, schema helpers
    Service testsDB writes, versioning, resets, permissions, status transitions
    Route testsHTTP contracts and error mapping
    Characterization testsProtect behavior during refactors
    Fixture testsRepresentative DOCX/PPTX/PDF/XLSX files
    Golden outputsStable expected outputs for deterministic stages
    LLM evalsPrompt quality and regression tracking
    Manual QA scriptsEnd-to-end consultant workflows

    For LLM-heavy flows, do not rely only on live model tests. Keep deterministic seams:

    • Parser helpers.
    • Prompt input assembly.
    • Structured-output validation.
    • Post-processing and calculation logic.
    • Persistence and status updates.

    Observability

    Observability should answer two questions: what happened operationally, and where did users need to correct the agent? Both are required to improve reliability and product quality.

    Operational telemetryJob, stage, model, duration, retry count, error type, degraded count, source files.
    Product telemetryUser edits, repeated questions, parse failures, low-confidence dimensions, reruns, abandonment.

    The minimum useful telemetry for agentic diagnostics:

    • Job ID.
    • Case/process IDs.
    • Stage name.
    • Model/provider.
    • Prompt/input size estimate.
    • Output token estimate where available.
    • Duration.
    • Retry count.
    • Error type.
    • Degraded/partial failure count.
    • Source files involved.

    Avoid logging raw prompt content unless explicitly enabled for a safe development environment.

    For product improvement, track:

    • How often users edit agent outputs.
    • Which questions agents ask most often.
    • Which files fail parsing.
    • Which dimensions/KPIs have low confidence.
    • Which stages are most frequently re-run.
    • Where users abandon the workflow.

    What Other Teams Should Reuse

    The safest guidance is not “copy the repo.” Copy the product patterns, adapt the domain workflow, and avoid carrying forward known debt like in-memory-only job state or provider calls without policy.

    CopyTyped stage contracts, evidence traceability, validation states, dry-run/publish/versioning.
    AdaptLangGraph, Data Manager, SSE events, parsing, prompts, and concurrency limits.
    AvoidGod-classes, unsafe re-runs, scattered SDK calls, and production reliance on volatile memory.

    Good patterns to copy:

    • Product-specific workflows instead of generic chat.
    • Typed schemas between every stage.
    • Evidence traceability back to source files.
    • Human validation states.
    • Admin dry-run / publish / versioning flows.
    • Next.js API proxy pattern.
    • In-process agents for low-latency streaming when operationally acceptable.
    • Characterization tests before large service refactors.

    Adapt with care:

    • LangGraph stage layout.
    • Data Manager model.
    • File parsing pipeline.
    • SSE event model.
    • LLM concurrency limits.
    • Prompt and rubric structure.

    Avoid copying blindly:

    • In-memory-only job tracking for production workflows.
    • Direct provider calls without a shared abstraction, timeout, retry, and observability policy.
    • Human-numbered Alembic migration filenames without CI head checks.
    • Long route or service god-classes.
    • Re-run flows that delete validated user work without an explicit confirmation or rollback path.

    FAQ for Other Teams

    Use this FAQ as the handoff layer for teams deciding whether to reuse the pattern, where to draw boundaries, and what to decide before starting.

    Product shapeWhy not just chat? When should users be asked?
    ArchitectureWhy in-process agents? When LangGraph?
    OperationsToken cost, provider path, persistent state, quality gates.

    Why not just build a chatbot?

    Because consultants need structured, defensible outputs: scores, ranges, evidence, baselines, benchmarks, and actions. Chat is useful as an interaction style, but the durable product output should be typed and reviewable.

    Why run agents in the backend process?

    It keeps streaming and human-in-the-loop interactions simpler. The backend can orchestrate the agent and emit progress events without a separate network hop. The tradeoff is that agent work consumes backend resources, so concurrency controls and job isolation become important.

    When should we use LangGraph?

    Use LangGraph when the workflow has clear stages and shared state. Do not use it just because an LLM is involved. Simple classification or one-shot extraction may only need a service function with a structured-output call.

    When should we ask the user a question?

    Ask when the ambiguity affects business correctness and cannot be safely inferred. Good questions are narrow, answerable, and tied to the next action. Bad questions ask the user to debug the agent.

    How do we keep token costs under control?

    Constrain context by stage, chunk large files, use only relevant rubric sections, log token estimates, limit concurrency, and avoid re-running downstream stages unnecessarily. Also make reset/regenerate actions explicit so users do not accidentally trigger expensive work.

    Should we use direct Anthropic/OpenAI APIs or Bedrock?

    This depends on enterprise requirements, model availability, operational controls, and data-boundary constraints. If portability matters, build a provider abstraction early. Do not scatter direct SDK calls across the codebase if you expect to switch providers.

    What is the biggest hidden complexity?

    State. Not prompts. The hard part is managing files, parsed evidence, user validation, derived outputs, re-runs, stale states, partial failures, and recovery after interruptions.

    What should be persistent?

    Anything needed to explain, resume, audit, or repair a workflow:

    • Uploaded files.
    • Parse metadata.
    • Evidence.
    • Agent outputs.
    • User decisions.
    • Job/stage status.
    • Prompt/model/version metadata for important outputs.

    Ephemeral UI progress can be in memory or SSE, but the durable workflow state should be in the database.

    How do we know an LLM result is good enough?

    Use a combination of schema validation, source traceability, confidence signals, deterministic post-checks, and human validation. The LLM should produce candidates; the product should make correctness reviewable.

    What should be decided before other teams start?

    • Which provider path is approved.
    • Which shared agent patterns are blessed.
    • Whether job state must be durable from day one.
    • What file types are supported.
    • How client data retention works.
    • How admin-managed knowledge is maintained.
    • Which telemetry is mandatory.
    • Which components are reusable versus project-specific.

    Suggested Onboarding Agenda for Other Teams

    Use this structure for a 60-90 minute walkthrough:

    1. Product framing: diagnostic workflow, not generic chat.
    2. Reference architecture: frontend, backend, agents, DB, files, LLM.
    3. Demo one structured pipeline and one human-in-the-loop flow.
    4. Explain data lifecycle: upload -> parse -> evidence -> output -> validation.
    5. Discuss LLM mechanics: prompts, tokens, concurrency, provider choices.
    6. Walk through watch-outs: job state, partial failures, migrations, parsing.
    7. Clarify what teams can reuse and what they should redesign.
    8. Align on open decisions for future teams.

    Open Decisions / Follow-ups

    These are worth aligning before many teams start copying the pattern:

    • Do we want a shared provider abstraction for Anthropic/OpenAI/Bedrock?
    • What is the standard timeout and retry policy for LLM calls?
    • Should all long-running agent jobs use a database-backed job table?
    • What telemetry is mandatory for token usage and cost visibility?
    • Which admin-managed knowledge flows should be reusable components?
    • How should teams handle migration head collisions in CI?
    • What is the minimum human-validation model for diagnostics that produce client-facing recommendations?
